source.title: Multi-Head Finite Automata: Characterizations, Concepts and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: For each fixed number of heads k >= 2, are nondeterministic two-way k-head finite automata strictly more powerful than deterministic two-way k-head finite automata, or can every language accepted by a nondeterministic two-way k-head finite automaton also be accepted by some deterministic two-way k-head finite automaton with the same number of heads? Equivalently, is the inclusion L(2DFA(k)) subseteq L(2NFA(k)) proper for fixed k in the two-way setting?
accepted.context_brief: Determinism versus nondeterminism for two-way multi-head automata

evidence.quote: Theorem 5. Let k ≥ 1. Then there are unary languages that show the inclusions L (2DFA(k)) ⊂ L (2DFA(k+1)) and L (2NFA(k)) ⊂ L (2NFA(k+1)). Whether nondeterminism is better than determinism in the two-way setting, is an open problem.
In fact, in [44] it was shown that the equality for at least one k ≥ 2 implies L = NL.

accepted.question_text: What is the exact state complexity of simulating a nondeterministic two-way one-head finite automaton by a deterministic two-way one-head finite automaton? More precisely, given a 2NFA(1), how many states are sufficient and how many are necessary in the worst case for an equivalent 2DFA(1)?

evidence.quote: Nevertheless, some challenging problems of finite automata are still open. An important example is the question of how many states are sufficient and necessary to simulate 2NFA(1) with 2DFA(1); we refer to [12, 23, 39, 41] for further reading.

accepted.question_text: For one-way data-independent (oblivious) multi-head finite automata, is the hierarchy by number of heads strict at every adjacent level? That is, for every k >= 1, does allowing k+1 heads recognize strictly more languages than allowing only k heads?
accepted.context_brief: Strictness of the one-way data-independent head hierarchy

evidence.quote: Whether the one-way hierarchy for data-independent multi-head finite automata is strict in the sense that k + 1 heads are better than k, is an open problem.

Finally, the most interesting point for research might be (3) the one-way k-head hierarchy for data-independent finite automata. Is it a strict hierarchy, in the sense that k+1 heads are better than k?

accepted.question_text: Determine tight conversion bounds between one-head data-independent finite automata and one-head data-dependent finite automata. In particular, when a language is recognized by a one-head data-independent finite automaton, what description-size blow-up is required to convert it into an equivalent one-head data-dependent deterministic, nondeterministic, or alternating finite automaton, and what bounds hold in the reverse direction?
accepted.context_brief: Conversion bounds between one-head data-independent and data-dependent automata

evidence.quote: We close this subsection by mentioning some open problems for further research: (1) Determine the bounds of the conversions of one-head data-independent finite automata into one-head data-dependent deterministic, nondeterministic, and alternating finite automata and vice versa.

accepted.question_text: For k-head data-independent finite automata, determine the decidability status and computational complexity of basic decision problems such as equivalence and non-emptiness. More generally, which standard semantic decision problems are decidable for these automata, and what are their exact complexity bounds?
accepted.context_brief: Decision problems for k-head data-independent automata

evidence.quote: We close this subsection by mentioning some open problems for further research: (2) Consider decidability and complexity questions such as equivalence, non-emptiness, etc. for k-head data-independent finite automata.
